demographics.trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another

Triggers.value: Undergoing a medical examination or procedure

Maladaptive Strategies.value: keep mind occupied all the time

Threat.value: I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert
Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame
Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience

Memory.value: The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over
When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once
I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it

Negative Appraisals.value: I can't trust that I will do the right thing
My life has been destroyed by the trauma
The event happened because of the way I acted

issues.item: Memory: Verbal Access: I can talk about what happened very easily.
issues.explanation: Within Memory, 'Feels Present Not Past' and 'Full Sensory Reliving' indicate highly intrusive, poorly contextualized trauma memory, which conflicts with 'Verbal Access: I can talk about what happened very easily.' These can sometimes coexist, but stated this strongly they pull in opposite directions and are hard to reconcile as the same memory profile.

issues.item: Threat: Watching Others: I watch other people closely for signs that they might harm me
issues.explanation: The Threat items depict pervasive fear of being physically attacked by other people ('watch other people closely', 'back to wall', 'stay alert at night'), which does not fit well with the trauma type of accidentally causing serious injury to another. For this trauma, threat is more plausibly guilt, condemnation, or fear of consequences, not generalized interpersonal danger.

issues.item: Threat: Back to Wall: I feel unsafe unless my back is against a wall where I can see the room
issues.explanation: 'Mirror Checking' is not well linked to the rest of the profile. Nothing in Triggers, Memory, Threat, or Negative Appraisals suggests appearance-focused concern, dissociation needing visual reassurance, or checking for injury; as selected, it appears clinically disconnected.

Mirror checking is hard to reconcile with the trauma type of accidentally causing serious injury to another; it more strongly suggests concerns about visible injury, appearance, or being followed, none of which are supported by the other nodes.

issues.item: Back to Wall: I feel unsafe unless my back is against a wall where I can see the room
issues.explanation: Back-to-wall hypervigilance and scanning the room imply an interpersonal or attack-related threat context. That is difficult to integrate with the rest of the profile, which centers on guilt, reliving, and self-blame after accidentally injuring someone rather than danger from other people.

vignette:
Chris, a 34-year-old school counselor, had always prided himself on his calm demeanor and ability to navigate complex situations with a clear head. That self-image shattered irrevocably on a Tuesday evening two years ago. He was driving home, his mind still buzzing from a particularly challenging parent-teacher conference, when his phone buzzed with a notification. Though he didn't look at it, the sudden sound momentarily diverted his attention. In that split second, a pedestrian stepped into the crosswalk. The screech of tires, the sickening thud, and the sight of the person lying motionless on the asphalt seared themselves into his mind. He remembered the metallic tang of blood in the air, the acrid smell of burnt rubber, and the blare of sirens as emergency services arrived. He watched, horrified, as paramedics worked frantically, the injured person’s still form a stark, agonizing testament to his momentary lapse. Chris was certain that the event happened because of the way he acted, a belief that gnawed at him relentlessly, convincing him he couldn't trust that he would ever do the right thing again.

Since that night, Chris’s world had shrunk, overshadowed by a constant sense of dread and guilt. Memories of the accident would ambush him without warning, feeling less like recollections and more like a full sensory reliving. He would be back in that moment, the sounds, the smells, the horrific visual details assaulting him as if it were happening right then, not something that was over and done with. When he tried to articulate these experiences, the words would fail him; he knew what happened but was unable to find words to describe it, leaving him feeling isolated and misunderstood.

His job, once a source of fulfillment, had become a minefield of triggers. The general stress of managing a busy school counseling caseload, with its constant demands and emotional intensity, often served as a potent cue. A particularly fraught meeting with an upset parent, or the pressure of a tight deadline, would frequently usher in a wave of strong physical reactions: his heart would pound, his palms would sweat, and a suffocating tightness would grip his chest. The smell of antiseptic from the school nurse’s office, or even the faint scent of exhaust fumes from buses in the parking lot, could instantly transport him back to the scene of the accident, triggering the same intense fear, horror, and profound shame.

To cope, Chris had developed a rigid set of routines. He made sure to keep his mind occupied all the time, filling every waking hour with tasks, hobbies, or endless scrolling through his phone. He would stay late at work, volunteer for extra committees, anything to avoid the quiet moments when thoughts about the event might creep in. This constant mental distraction left him exhausted, and his wife, Sarah, had noticed his increasing emotional distance. He also found himself actively avoiding any situation that might involve police, taking circuitous routes to work to bypass a police station, or immediately changing the channel if a news report featured law enforcement. He just couldn't bear the association.

Sleep offered no respite. He had difficulty falling asleep because he needed to stay alert, constantly listening for sounds, his mind racing with hypothetical dangers, convinced that another catastrophe was always just around the corner. He would lie awake for hours, his hyper-vigilance leaving him perpetually drained. He had come to believe that his life had been destroyed by the trauma, a deep-seated conviction that fueled his pervasive negative emotions – the crushing guilt, the persistent fear, and a profound sense of hopelessness that made it hard to imagine a future where he felt whole again. The cumulative toll of these two years had finally become unbearable, prompting Sarah to gently, but firmly, suggest he seek help. Chris arrived at therapy feeling utterly depleted, yet still clinging to the hope, however faint, that someone might be able to help him escape the prison of his own mind. What frightened him most was the possibility that even professional help wouldn't be enough to undo the damage he felt he had wrought, both to himself and to another.
